1:5.t: "Seventy": the Greek Old Testament and a Dead Sea Scroll read seventy-five, as quoted in Acts 7:14.

1:11.t: Rameses: the KJV spells it Raamses here.

1:21.t: "Families of their own": the KJV's "he made them houses".

2:3.t: "Basket": the KJV's "ark", the same Hebrew word as Noah's ark (tevah), used only in these two stories.

2:10.t: Moses sounds like the Hebrew for "draw out".

3:1.t: "Far side": the KJV's "backside", meaning the west side.

3:22.t: "Ask": the KJV's "borrow". The Hebrew means to ask for; nothing was to be returned.

4:2.t: "Staff": the KJV's "rod", a shepherd's walking stick.

4:6.t: "Diseased, white as snow": the KJV's "leprous as snow". The Hebrew word (tsara'at) covers various skin diseases, not only what is called leprosy today.

4:24.t: "A place where they stopped for the night": the KJV's "the inn".

4:25.t: "Touched his feet with it": the KJV's "cast it at his feet". Whose feet, Moses' or the boy's, is not clear in the Hebrew.

6:12.t: "Speak so poorly": the KJV's "of uncircumcised lips".

6:30.t: "Speak so poorly": the KJV's "of uncircumcised lips".

6:17.t: Shimei, Mahli, Sithri: the KJV spells them Shimi, Mahali, Zithri. 6:23 Nahshon: the KJV spells it Naashon.

7:1.t: "Like God": the KJV's "a god". Moses will speak with God's authority, and Aaron will speak for him as a prophet speaks for God.

7:13.t: "Pharaoh's heart was hardened": the KJV reads "he hardened", but the Hebrew verb here has no stated subject.

7:19.t: "Canals": the KJV's "rivers", the channels of the Nile.

8:5.t: "Canals": the KJV's "rivers", the channels of the Nile.

8:9.t: "I leave to you the honor of setting the time": the KJV's "Glory over me".

8:16.t: "Gnats": the KJV's "lice". The Hebrew word may mean gnats, lice or mosquitoes.

8:21.t: "Flies": the Hebrew says only "swarms"; the KJV supplies "of flies".

9:3.t: "Plague": the KJV's "murrain", an old word for a cattle disease.

9:9.t: "Festering boils": the KJV's "a boil breaking forth with blains", blisters.

9:32.t: "Spelt": the KJV's "rie", a kind of wheat.

10:4.t: "Territory", "every part of it", "anywhere in Egypt": the KJV's "coast" and "coasts", meaning borders or territory.

10:14.t: "Territory", "every part of it", "anywhere in Egypt": the KJV's "coast" and "coasts", meaning borders or territory.

10:19.t: "Territory", "every part of it", "anywhere in Egypt": the KJV's "coast" and "coasts", meaning borders or territory.
"Red Sea": the Hebrew is yam suph, "Sea of Reeds". The KJV follows the Greek Old Testament in calling it the Red Sea.

10:10.t: "The LORD be with you if I ever let you go": Pharaoh is being sarcastic.

11:5.t: "Hand mill": the KJV's "behind the mill", the lowest of household tasks.

11:7.t: "Growl": the KJV's "move his tongue", that is, bark or snarl.

12:6.t: "At twilight": the KJV's "in the evening"; the Hebrew is "between the two evenings".

12:11.t: "With your belt fastened": the KJV's "with your loins girded", ready to travel.

"Passover" (Hebrew pesach): from the verb pasach, "to pass over" or "to protect by hovering over", used in verses 13, 23 and 27. The Greek form, pascha, gives the word Paschal. The New Testament calls Christ "our Passover lamb" (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John notes that none of His bones were broken (John 19:36, quoting 12:46).

12:37.t: "600,000 men": the Hebrew word elef, usually "thousand", may also mean a clan or military unit, which some take to mean a smaller total.

12:40.t: "430 years": the Greek Old Testament and the Samaritan text count the 430 years as the time in Canaan and Egypt together, as Paul does in Galatians 3:17.

13:4.t: Abib: the first month, March to April, later called Nisan.

13:9.t: "A sign on your hand and a band on your forehead": the KJV's "frontlets between thine eyes". Later Jewish practice took this literally, as the tefillin, small boxes holding Scripture.

13:16.t: "A sign on your hand and a band on your forehead": the KJV's "frontlets between thine eyes". Later Jewish practice took this literally, as the tefillin, small boxes holding Scripture.

13:12.t: "First offspring of every womb": the KJV's "all that openeth the matrix".

13:15.t: "First offspring of every womb": the KJV's "all that openeth the matrix".

13:18.t: "Ready for battle": the KJV's "harnessed", in the old sense of armed or in formation.

14:24.t: "The last watch of the night": the KJV's "the morning watch", from about two to six in the morning.

14:25.t: "Made the wheels come off": the KJV's "took off their chariot wheels". The Greek Old Testament reads "clogged" or "bound", meaning the wheels stuck.

15:2.t: "I will praise Him": the KJV's "I will prepare him an habitation". The Hebrew verb is rare; it may mean either.

15:13.t: "Will lead": the Hebrew verbs in verses 13-17 can be read as past or future; the song looks ahead to the journey to the promised land.
"Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): the KJV's "mercy". See Genesis 24:27.

15:24.t: "Grumbled": the KJV's "murmured", used often in Exodus and Numbers for Israel's complaining.

15:25.t: "A piece of wood": the KJV's "a tree"; the Hebrew word means both.

16:1.t: "Wilderness of Sin": a place name, unrelated to the English word sin.

16:34.t: "The Testimony": the tablets of the covenant law, later kept in the ark (25:16).

16:36.t: An ephah is about 22 liters, so an omer is about 2.2 liters.

17:7.t: "Put the LORD to the test" (Hebrew nasah): the KJV's "tempt". To test God means to demand that He prove Himself. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:16, which recalls this event, in Matthew 4:7.

17:16.t: "Because a hand was raised against the throne of the LORD": the KJV reads "Because the LORD hath sworn". The Hebrew is difficult; the KJV margin gives "the hand upon the throne of the LORD", which may mean God's hand raised in an oath or Amalek's hand raised against God.

18:2.t: "Sent his wife Zipporah away": when or why is not said; compare 4:20-26.

18:21.t: "Dishonest gain": the KJV's "covetousness", here meaning bribes.

19:13.t: "Ram's horn" and "trumpet": verse 13 uses yobel, a ram's horn; verses 16 and 19 use shofar, also a horn trumpet.

19:16.t: "Ram's horn" and "trumpet": verse 13 uses yobel, a ram's horn; verses 16 and 19 use shofar, also a horn trumpet.

19:19.t: "Ram's horn" and "trumpet": verse 13 uses yobel, a ram's horn; verses 16 and 19 use shofar, also a horn trumpet.
"With thunder": the Hebrew qol means both "voice" and "thunder". The KJV has "by a voice".

19:15.t: "Do not have sexual relations with a woman": the KJV's "come not at your wives".

20:2.t: Jews and Christians number the Ten Commandments differently. Some count verse 2 as the first "word"; some join verses 3-6; some divide verse 17 into two.

20:24.t: "Peace offerings": a sacrifice shared between God, the priests and the worshiper in a meal.

21:6.t: "Before God": the KJV's "unto the judges". The Hebrew is ha'elohim, "God", which may mean before God at the sanctuary or before judges acting for Him.

21:8.t: "Chosen her for himself": the KJV's "betrothed her to himself". A different Hebrew reading gives "so that he has not chosen her".

21:22.t: "Her child is born early": the KJV's "her fruit depart from her". The Hebrew can mean an early live birth or a miscarriage. "Further harm" (the KJV's "mischief") may refer to the mother, the child, or both.

21:25.t: "Bruise": the KJV's "stripe", a mark left by a blow.

22:2.t: "At night": the Hebrew does not say "at night", but verse 3 ("after sunrise") shows that is the meaning. The KJV's "breaking up" means breaking in.

22:8.t: "Before God": the KJV's "unto the judges", as at 21:6.

22:16.t: "Bride-price": the KJV's "endow her" and "the dowry of virgins", a payment from the groom to the bride's father.

22:25.t: "Interest": the KJV's "usury", which once meant any interest at all, not only excessive interest.

22:29.t: "Your wine and oil": the KJV's "thy liquors"; the Hebrew means "your juice", from the winepress and olive press.

23:16.t: The Festival of Harvest is later called the Festival of Weeks, or Pentecost; the Festival of Ingathering is later called the Festival of Booths, or Tabernacles.

23:24.t: "Sacred pillars": the KJV's "images", standing stones used in Canaanite worship.

23:28.t: "The hornet": the Hebrew may mean an actual hornet or a picture of panic.

24:10.t: "Sapphire": possibly lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.
"They saw the God of Israel": compare 33:20, "no one can see Me and live". What they saw is described only by what was under His feet. The text tells of a real meeting while guarding God's holiness.

25:3.t: "Bronze": the KJV's "brass". Ancient "brass" was bronze, copper alloyed with tin.

25:5.t: "Fine leather": the KJV's "badgers' skins". The Hebrew tachash is uncertain; suggestions include dolphin or sea cow skin, or a fine dyed leather. "Acacia": the KJV's "shittim wood", from the Hebrew name of the tree.

25:7.t: "Breastpiece": the KJV's "breastplate", a pouch worn by the high priest (28:15-30).

25:10.t: KJV: "two cubits and a half" long, "a cubit and a half" wide and high.

25:12.t: "Feet": the KJV's "corners"; the Hebrew word usually means feet.

25:17.t: KJV: "two cubits and a half" by "a cubit and a half".

"Mercy seat" (Hebrew kapporet): from kaphar, "to cover" or "to make atonement". It was the gold lid of the ark, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14). Many modern Bibles call it the "atonement cover"; we keep the KJV's well-known term, which comes from Tyndale. The Greek Old Testament calls it hilasterion, the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25.

25:23.t: KJV: "two cubits" long, "a cubit" wide, "a cubit and a half" high. 25:25 KJV: "an hand breadth".

25:30.t: "Bread of the Presence": the KJV's "shewbread", literally "bread of the face", set before God.

25:31.t: "Lampstand": the KJV's "candlestick". It held oil lamps, not candles. "Buds": the KJV's "knops".

26:2.t: KJV: twenty-eight cubits by four cubits. 26:8 KJV: thirty cubits by four. 26:13 KJV: "a cubit". 26:16 KJV: ten cubits by a cubit and a half.

26:15.t: "Frames": the KJV's "boards". 26:17 "Pegs": the KJV's "tenons". 26:19 "Bases": the KJV's "sockets".

26:31.t: "Curtain": the KJV's "vail". This is the curtain that tore in two when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51).

26:33.t: "The Holy Place ... the Most Holy Place": the KJV's "the holy place and the most holy", literally "the holy of holies".

27:1.t: KJV: five cubits long and wide, three cubits high. 27:9-18 KJV: courtyard 100 by 50 cubits; side curtains fifteen cubits; entrance screen twenty cubits; height five cubits.

27:10.t: "Bands": the KJV's "fillets", connecting rods or bands on the posts.

27:21.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation". The Hebrew ohel mo'ed means the tent where God meets with His people.

28:4.t: "Tunic": the KJV's "coat". "Turban": the KJV's "mitre". "Sash": the KJV's "girdle".

28:8.t: "Waistband": the KJV's "curious girdle", meaning a skillfully made belt.

28:17.t: Several of these gems cannot be identified with certainty, and the KJV's names (sardius, carbuncle, ligure) differ from modern ones. We give likely modern equivalents.

29:13.t: "Lobe of the liver": the KJV's "the caul that is above the liver".

29:22.t: "Fat tail": the KJV's "rump", from a breed of sheep with a broad fatty tail.

29:27.t: "Presented": the KJV's "heave offering", a portion lifted up and set apart for God and the priests.

29:40.t: KJV: "a tenth deal of flour" (a tenth of an ephah) and "the fourth part of an hin" of oil and of wine.

30:2.t: KJV: "a cubit" long and wide, "two cubits" high.

30:9.t: "Unauthorized incense": the KJV's "strange incense", incense not made by the formula in 30:34-35.

30:13.t: KJV: "half a shekel after the shekel of the sanctuary". A gerah is about 0.6 grams.

30:23.t: KJV: myrrh and cassia "five hundred shekels" each, cinnamon and calamus "two hundred and fifty shekels" each, and "an hin" of oil.

30:34.t: "Gum resin": the KJV's "stacte", a drop resin. Onycha may be a fragrant shell; galbanum is a plant resin.

30:35.t: "Salted": the KJV's "tempered together". The Hebrew word means salted.

31:2.t: Bezalel: the KJV spells it Bezaleel. 31:6 Oholiab: the KJV spells it Aholiab.

31:10.t: "Woven garments": the KJV's "cloths of service". The Hebrew word is uncertain.

32:4.t: "Shaped it with a tool": the Hebrew may also mean "tied it in a bag".

"Gods" (Hebrew elohim): the word can mean "God" or "gods". The people may have meant the calf as an image of the LORD, since Aaron calls the feast "a festival to the LORD" (32:5). Even so, it broke the second commandment (20:4). Jeroboam repeats the same words in 1 Kings 12:28.

32:6.t: "Indulge in revelry": the KJV's "rose up to play". The Hebrew verb can include sexual play (compare Genesis 26:8). Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 10:7.

32:18.t: "Victory ... defeat": the KJV's "them that shout for mastery ... them that cry for being overcome".

32:25.t: "Running wild": the KJV's "naked". The Hebrew word means let loose or out of control.

33:7.t: "Used to take": the Hebrew describes a regular practice. This tent was a temporary meeting place before the tabernacle was built.

34:13.t: "Asherah poles": the KJV's "groves". Asherah was a Canaanite goddess, worshiped at wooden poles or trees.

34:15.t: "Prostitute themselves": the KJV's "go a whoring". The Old Testament often pictures idolatry as unfaithfulness in marriage.

34:29.t: "Shining": the Hebrew verb qaran comes from qeren, "horn". The Latin Vulgate read it as "horned", which is why some old art, including Michelangelo's statue, shows Moses with horns.

34:35.t: "Shining": the Hebrew verb qaran comes from qeren, "horn". The Latin Vulgate read it as "horned", which is why some old art, including Michelangelo's statue, shows Moses with horns.

34:33.t: "Veil": the KJV's "vail". Paul draws on this passage in 2 Corinthians 3:7-18.

35:22.t: "Brooches": the KJV's "bracelets"; "ornaments": the KJV's "tablets". The exact items are uncertain.

35:35.t: Most modern Bibles begin chapter 36 in the middle of Moses' speech, as the KJV does. We follow the KJV's verse division.

36:38.t: "Tops": the KJV's "chapiters", the capitals of the posts.

38:8.t: "Mirrors": the KJV's "lookingglasses", polished bronze mirrors. "Served": the Hebrew word (tsava) is used of service at the sanctuary; compare 1 Samuel 2:22.

38:24.t: KJV: "twenty and nine talents, and seven hundred and thirty shekels" of gold.

38:25.t: KJV: "an hundred talents, and a thousand seven hundred and threescore and fifteen shekels" of silver; "a talent for a socket".

38:26.t: A bekah is half a shekel, about 5.7 grams. The total, 603,550, matches the census in Numbers 1:46.

38:29.t: KJV: "seventy talents, and two thousand and four hundred shekels" of bronze.

40:17.t: The first month of the second year, about a year after leaving Egypt.

40:38.t: "In the cloud": the KJV's "on it". The Hebrew reads "in it".

3:14.t: "I AM WHO I AM" (Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh): ehyeh is the verb "to be" in a form that can mean "I am" or "I will be". So the phrase can also be read "I will be who I will be" or "I am the One who is". It tells Moses that God exists by Himself, depends on no one, and will be present with His people. The name YHWH in verse 15, printed LORD, comes from the same verb (see Genesis 2:4). Jesus' "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58) echoes this verse.

3:15.t: "How I am to be remembered" (Hebrew zeker): the KJV's "memorial", the name by which God is to be called on.

4:21.t: "Harden his heart" (Hebrew chazaq, "make strong"; also kabed, "make heavy", and qashah, "make stubborn"): the story uses all three verbs. Sometimes God hardens Pharaoh's heart (4:21, 9:12), sometimes Pharaoh hardens his own (8:15, 8:32), and sometimes it simply "was hardened" (7:13). The heart in Hebrew is the seat of thought and will, not only feeling. The text holds God's sovereignty and Pharaoh's responsibility together without resolving them; Paul takes up the question in Romans 9:17-18.

6:3.t: "Yahweh" (Hebrew YHWH): one of the places where the KJV prints JEHOVAH, so the name is spelled out here (see Genesis 2:4). The verse does not mean the patriarchs never heard the name, which appears often in Genesis, but that they had not known God in the full sense the name carries: the One who keeps His promises and redeems His people.

6:6.t: "Redeem" (Hebrew ga'al): to buy back or rescue as a family member. The go'el was the relative who bought back land, freed a kinsman from slavery, or avenged his blood (Leviticus 25:25, Ruth 3:9). God here acts as Israel's next of kin.

9:16.t: "Raised you up" (Hebrew he'emadtikha, "caused you to stand"): it can mean "kept you alive" or "set you in your place". Paul quotes the verse in Romans 9:17 as "for this very purpose I raised you up", stressing God's purpose in history.

12:15.t: "Cut off" (Hebrew karat): the phrase may mean being put to death, being expelled from the community, or God Himself ending the person's line. The Law does not say which in each case.

"Yeast" (Hebrew se'or, chamets): the KJV's "leaven", a lump of old fermented dough used to make new dough rise. Unleavened bread (matstsah) recalled the haste of leaving Egypt. Later, yeast becomes a picture of the way sin or false teaching spreads (Matthew 16:6, 1 Corinthians 5:6-8).

12:23.t: "The destroyer" (Hebrew hammashchit): a destroying agent sent by God, elsewhere called an angel (2 Samuel 24:16). The text does not say more about who or what it is.

12:38.t: "Mixed crowd" (Hebrew erev rav): people who were not descended from Jacob, Egyptians and others, who left Egypt with Israel.

13:13.t: "Redeem" (Hebrew padah): to buy back by paying a price. Here a lamb is the price for a donkey's life, and a payment (Numbers 18:16) for a firstborn son. Compare ga'al, the family redeemer, at 6:6.

14:13.t: "Deliverance" (Hebrew yeshuah): the KJV's "salvation". The word means rescue or victory, deliverance from real danger. The name Joshua (and its Greek form, Jesus) comes from the same root: "the LORD saves".

14:14.t: "Be still" (Hebrew charash): the KJV's "hold your peace". It means to be quiet and stop, not to stay passive forever; in verse 15 God tells them to move.

15:3.t: "Warrior" (Hebrew ish milchamah): the KJV's "a man of war". It describes God fighting for His people; it does not mean God has a human body.

15:11.t: "Among the gods" (Hebrew ba'elim): the song compares the LORD with the gods the nations worshiped, which the plagues had just humbled (12:12). It does not mean those gods were real rivals.

15:26.t: "The LORD who heals you" (Hebrew YHWH rophe'ekha): rapha means to heal, restore or make whole, used of bodies, land and nations. Some later traditions turned it into a title, Yahweh-Rapha, but here the KJV has "the LORD that healeth thee", so LORD is kept.

16:15.t: "What is it?" (Hebrew man hu): the KJV reads "It is manna", but the Hebrew man is the question "what?". The name manna (16:31) comes from that question. Jesus calls Himself "the true bread from heaven" with this story in mind (John 6:31-35).

16:23.t: "Sabbath" (Hebrew shabbat): from the verb shavat, "to stop" or "to rest", the same verb used of God resting in Genesis 2:2. This is the first time the word appears, before the Ten Commandments are given (20:8).

17:2.t: "Put the LORD to the test" (Hebrew nasah): the KJV's "tempt". To test God means to demand that He prove Himself. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:16, which recalls this event, in Matthew 4:7.

17:15.t: Yahweh-nissi (Hebrew YHWH nissi): the KJV prints Jehovah-nissi, "the LORD is my banner". A banner (nes) was a pole raised as a rallying point in battle, like Moses' raised staff in verse 9.

19:5.t: "Treasured possession" (Hebrew segullah): the KJV's "a peculiar treasure", where "peculiar" meant "belonging to one owner", not "odd". A king's segullah was his private treasure. 1 Peter 2:9 applies this verse and the next to the church.

19:6.t: "Kingdom of priests" (Hebrew mamlekhet kohanim): the whole nation was to stand between God and the other nations as priests stand between God and the people.

19:10.t: "Consecrate" (Hebrew qadash): to make holy or set apart for God. The KJV's "sanctify". Holy (qadosh) means set apart, belonging to God, and so pure.

20:3.t: "Before Me" (Hebrew al panai): literally "upon My face" or "in My presence". It can mean "besides Me", "in place of Me", or "in defiance of Me". The point is that no other god may share the place of the LORD.

20:4.t: "Carved image" (Hebrew pesel): the KJV's "graven image", an idol carved from wood or stone. The command forbids making images to worship, as verse 5 shows, not all art; the tabernacle itself had carved cherubim (25:18).

20:5.t: "Jealous" (Hebrew qanna): this is not petty envy but the rightful zeal of a husband who will not share his wife's love with another. The Old Testament often pictures idolatry as unfaithfulness in marriage (Hosea 2). "Punish" (paqad, the KJV's "visiting") means to attend to or bring to account. The punishment reaches "those who hate Me", children who continue in their fathers' sins (compare Ezekiel 18:20).

20:6.t: "Steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed): the KJV's "mercy". See Genesis 24:27. "Thousands" probably means "a thousand generations" (Deuteronomy 7:9), in contrast to the three or four generations of verse 5.

20:7.t: "Misuse" (Hebrew nasa lashav, "lift up for emptiness"): the KJV's "take in vain". It covers false oaths sworn in God's name, using His name for magic or deceit, and treating it as empty or worthless, not only careless speech.

20:13.t: "Murder" (Hebrew ratsach): the KJV's "kill". Hebrew has several words for killing. Ratsach is used for unlawful killing of a person, never for killing animals, killing in war, or lawful execution, which the next chapter commands (21:12). The KJV itself renders the command "Thou shalt do no murder" when Jesus quotes it (Matthew 19:18).

20:14.t: "Commit adultery" (Hebrew na'aph): sexual relations between a married person and someone other than his or her spouse.

20:16.t: "Give false testimony" (Hebrew ed shaqer, "a lying witness"): the setting is a court of law, though the principle reaches all lying about a neighbor.

20:17.t: "Covet" (Hebrew chamad): to desire something so strongly that one schemes to take it. This command reaches past actions to the heart. Paul says this command showed him his sin (Romans 7:7).

21:23.t: "Life for life, eye for eye" (Latin lex talionis): this law set a limit on punishment in the courts, so that it would match the injury and not exceed it. It was not permission for personal revenge, and payment could often take the place of injury (21:30). Jesus speaks to it in Matthew 5:38-39.

22:18.t: "Sorceress" (Hebrew mekhashephah): the KJV's "witch". The word means someone who practices sorcery or magic to harm or control others, the kind of practice that was common in Canaan (Deuteronomy 18:10). It does not describe what "witch" came to mean in later European witch hunts.

22:20.t: "Devoted to destruction" (Hebrew charam): the KJV's "utterly destroyed". Something under herem was handed over entirely to God, either for the sanctuary or for destruction, and could not be kept for personal use.

22:21.t: "Foreigner" (Hebrew ger): the KJV's "stranger". A ger was a foreigner living in Israel without family land or the protection of a clan. The Law repeatedly joins the ger with the widow and the orphan as people God Himself protects.

22:27.t: "Compassionate" (Hebrew channun): the KJV's "gracious". It describes kindness shown to someone who has no claim on it. See 34:6.

22:28.t: "God" (Hebrew elohim): the KJV reads "the gods". The word usually means God; some take it here to mean judges, who acted for God (as at 21:6). Paul quotes the second half of the verse in Acts 23:5.

23:19.t: "Boil a young goat in its mother's milk": the reason is not given. It may forbid a pagan rite, or teach respect for the bond between mother and young. Later Jewish law built the separation of meat and milk on this verse.

23:20.t: "An Angel ... My name is in Him": this messenger carries God's own authority and can forgive or withhold forgiveness, which God alone does. So He is capitalized here, as in the KJV. Many Christian readers identify Him with the angel of the LORD seen elsewhere.

24:8.t: "The blood of the covenant" (Hebrew dam habberit): the blood sealed the covenant, binding both parties to it. Jesus takes up these words at the Last Supper: "This is My blood of the new covenant" (Matthew 26:28, Hebrews 9:18-20).

25:8.t: "Sanctuary" (Hebrew miqdash, "holy place") and "tabernacle" (Hebrew mishkan, "dwelling place"): mishkan comes from shakan, "to dwell" or "to settle". The point of the whole tabernacle is in verse 8: "so that I may dwell among them". Compare John 1:14, "lived among us", literally "pitched His tent among us".

25:16.t: "The Testimony" (Hebrew edut): the stone tablets of the covenant, God's witness to the terms of His covenant with Israel. So the ark is called "the ark of the Testimony" and the tabernacle "the tabernacle of the Testimony".

25:18.t: "Cherubim" (Hebrew keruvim, plural of keruv): winged heavenly beings who guard God's holiness (Genesis 3:24) and surround His throne (Ezekiel 10). They are not the chubby infants of later art. Hebrew plurals end in -im, so the KJV's "cherubims" adds a needless English plural.

28:2.t: "Dignity and beauty" (Hebrew kavod and tif'eret): kavod, often "glory", comes from a word meaning weight or heaviness, so it suggests honor and importance. The priest's clothing showed the honor of his office before God.

28:15.t: "Breastpiece for making decisions" (Hebrew choshen mishpat): the KJV's "breastplate of judgment". Mishpat means judgment, justice, or a decision. The breastpiece held the Urim and Thummim, by which God's decisions were sought (Numbers 27:21).

28:30.t: "Urim and Thummim": the words probably mean "lights" and "perfections". They were objects kept in the breastpiece and used to learn God's will, perhaps by giving a yes or no answer (1 Samuel 14:41). How they worked is not described.

28:41.t: "Ordain" (Hebrew mille yad, "fill the hand"): the KJV's "consecrate". The phrase may come from placing the first offerings in the new priest's hands (29:24).

29:14.t: "Sin offering" (Hebrew chatta't): the same word means "sin" and the offering that deals with sin. Its main purpose was to purify the sanctuary and the worshiper from the defilement of sin. Paul may echo this double meaning in 2 Corinthians 5:21, "made Him to be sin for us".

29:18.t: "Pleasing aroma" (Hebrew reach nichoach, "soothing smell"): the KJV's "sweet savour". It means the offering is accepted by God. It does not mean God needs food. Paul uses the phrase of Christ's self-giving (Ephesians 5:2).

29:33.t: "Atonement" (Hebrew kaphar, kippurim): to make atonement means to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored. The root may mean "to cover" or "to wipe clean", and it is related to "ransom" (kopher). The English word itself was coined from "at one-ment", being made one with God.

29:45.t: "Dwell" (Hebrew shakan): the verb behind mishkan, "tabernacle" (see 25:8-9). The goal of the exodus is stated here: God freed Israel so that He might live among them.

32:9.t: "Stiff-necked" (Hebrew qesheh oref): a picture from farming: an ox that stiffens its neck and refuses the yoke. Stephen uses the same charge in Acts 7:51.

32:14.t: "Relented" (Hebrew nacham): the KJV's "repented". See Genesis 6:6. God did not change His character; He responded to Moses' prayer, as He had invited (32:10, "leave Me alone").

32:32.t: "Blot me out of the book": the book of the living, God's record of His people (Psalm 69:28, Revelation 3:5). Moses offers his own life for the people. Paul expresses a similar wish in Romans 9:3.

33:14.t: "My Presence" (Hebrew panai, "My face"): God's presence is spoken of as His face. Moses insists that only God's own presence, not an angel (33:2), can make Israel His people.

33:19.t: "I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious": the form echoes "I AM WHO I AM" (3:14). God's grace is His free choice, not something people can demand. Paul quotes the verse in Romans 9:15.

33:20.t: "My face ... My back": human language for what cannot be fully described. Moses is allowed to see the afterglow of God's passing, not His full glory. John 1:18 says no one has seen God, but the Son has made Him known.

34:6.t: God's self-description: this is the most quoted passage about God's character in the Old Testament (Numbers 14:18, Nehemiah 9:17, Psalm 86:15, 103:8, Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2). "Compassionate" (rachum) comes from rechem, "womb", a mother's tender love. "Gracious" (channun) is kindness to the undeserving. "Slow to anger" (erekh appayim) is literally "long of nostrils", taking a long time for anger to flare; the KJV's "longsuffering". "Steadfast love and faithfulness" (hesed ve'emet): see Genesis 24:27. "Wrongdoing, rebellion, and sin" (avon, pesha, chatta'ah) are the three main Hebrew words for evil: twisting, revolt, and missing the mark. Yet mercy is not the same as pretending guilt does not matter.

34:14.t: "Whose name is Jealous" (Hebrew qanna shemo): see 20:5. God's jealousy is His exclusive claim on His people's love, as in a marriage.

35:21.t: "Whose heart stirred him" (Hebrew nesa'o libbo, "whose heart lifted him"): the giving for the tabernacle was entirely voluntary, in contrast to the forced gold of the calf (32:2-3). Chapter 36:5-7 records that the people had to be told to stop giving.

35:31.t: "Skill" (Hebrew chokhmah): usually "wisdom". In the Old Testament wisdom includes practical skill in a craft, not only moral or intellectual insight. Bezalel is the first person in the Bible said to be filled with the Spirit of God.

40:34.t: "Glory" (Hebrew kavod): see 28:2. The glory that once rested on Sinai (24:16) now fills the tabernacle, and God's purpose stated in 25:8 and 29:45, to dwell among His people, is fulfilled. The same happens at Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10-11), and John 1:14 says, "We saw His glory."
"Settled" (Hebrew shakan): the verb behind mishkan, "tabernacle" (see 25:8-9). Later Jewish writers used the related word Shekinah for God's dwelling presence.
